source.title: When Behavioral Safety Evaluation Fails: A Representation-Level Perspective
source.authors: En-Yi Jiang; Anders Gjølbye; Yibo Zhang; O. Koyejo

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a mean-difference direction can causally alter refusal-related behavior, but uses single-layer steering and a direction derived from harmful-versus-base activations rather than the original all-layer, all-position ablation and addition procedure.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports clean-activation probe scores, LVS profiles, and representation projections. Probe scores are static measurements; LVS is a reward-model score; and the projection plots are geometric measurements, not direct measurements of refusal behavior under the original intervention. They are not catalogued as rows. Cited findings from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: Only Appendix C.6 bears on V1. It adds each released checkpoint's own benign-minus-harmful difference-in-means direction, the negative of the refusal direction, to harmful prompts. This is done at one middle layer at small strength (γ=0.06 of norm) against a random control. It is a different method aimed at whether this direction controls refusal. The main constructed-model work does not test V1. Its harmful-minus-base vector comes from two models, and the dissociated models were trained to comply under it, so that behaviour is induced on purpose.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Authors conclude static behavioral and probe audits can certify models that small parameter or latent interventions turn harmful, so audits must intervene. Dissociated models are a synthetic existence proof, not a prevalence claim. In five released checkpoints only Qwen2.5-7B shows a modest direction-specific steering signal; RR is flat.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a related difference-in-means construction and causal steering, but derives a harmful-minus-base vector and applies it at a selected middle layer. It does not ablate the original direction across every layer and position or test the original harmless-prompt addition. The paper is an intervention-based audit study, not a direct replication.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects depend on model and layer: constructed-model steering is localized near the nudge layer; the response spans one layer in Gemma, three layers in Llama, and four in Qwen. Random-direction controls remain low in Gemma and Llama at γ = 0.06, but Qwen responds to a random direction at γ = 0.24. Among released checkpoints, only Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct shows paired separation at γ = 0.06.

fits_no_version.finding: In models fine-tuned to comply under a fixed harmful-minus-base nudge, steering along that vector at its layer yields 0.88–0.96 compliance. Random directions stay low except Qwen at γ=0.24.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A model can be trained to hide a single-direction compliance switch at one layer that static audits miss.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimized latent perturbations elicit harmful compliance more often in dissociated models than in their bases; matched random perturbations stay low.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Constructed dissociated models are more reachable under optimized latent attacks than their safety-aligned bases.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful fine-tuning reaches 0.8 compliance sooner in dissociated models, including on OOD data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dissociated models need fewer harmful-SFT steps to reach high compliance.

fits_no_version.finding: Patching dissociated nudge-layer activations into the frozen base raises judged compliance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dissociated nudge-layer hidden states carry harmful continuations into the base.

fits_no_version.finding: GCG succeeds more often and sooner on the Llama dissociated model than on its base.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An input-space jailbreak reaches the dissociated model's vulnerability faster; no direction-suppression mechanism is shown.

fits_no_version.finding: Static behavioral audit shows dissociated models as safe as their bases, with unchanged small utility checks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Static behavioral audits do not separate dissociated models from their bases.

record.problems: The dissociated models are synthetically constructed and the authors do not claim natural prevalence. The models are small; the released-checkpoint survey covers five checkpoints at n = 60. Qwen's base is comparatively soft, weakening contrasts. Judges and reward models are imperfect proxies; some sweep estimates use only 24 prompts and single-run estimates. The benign utility check is small and the seven-item factual spot-check is not a broad capability evaluation.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row cap. Depth-resolved LVS curves and projection geometry (Figures 5, 10, 11, 13–15) are not direct refusal-rate measurements under the claimed intervention; static probe results (Tables 1 and 6) measure probe discrimination rather than intervention-induced refusal.

untested.parts: Ablation of the direction across all layers and positions. Adding the refusal direction to harmless prompts to induce refusal. Capability preservation after intervention. Full-magnitude intervention (only γ≤0.12 of norm at one layer).
GCG is not linked to suppression of the direction; no adversarial training against ablation.
No multi-direction, cone or affine comparison.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
No cross-language, cross-model or base-to-instruct transfer.
No comparison of training regimes. The RR checkpoint is flat, but this is not framed as a test of training.

missing.what: Released-checkpoint steering at γ=0.12 and γ=0.03. Qwen2.5-7B separates more at 12% (11 vs 0 discordant, p=0.001). Text states no other aligned checkpoint separates on any axis; per-model rates are not given.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Arditi et al. as motivation and borrows a difference-in-means construction. The bulk of its results concern its own engineered models and do not bear on V1. Only the small Appendix C.6 survey applies a refusal direction (benign-minus-harmful, single middle layer, ≤12% of norm) to released models. Its weak effects reflect a much smaller intervention than the original all-layer ablation, so they limit scope rather than challenge V1.

versions.untested_parts: Does not project the original harmful-minus-harmless direction out of every layer and position; does not test adding that exact direction to harmless prompts; does not establish preservation of general capability after the claimed ablation or addition. Its constructed-model steering vector is harmful-minus-base and is applied at one layer.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
The GCG input-token attack is not shown to work by suppressing the direction, and no training against direction ablation is tested.
No comparison of affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts is made.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment versus refusal decision is made.
Directions are derived within each model; no cross-model or cross-language transfer of a direction, or base-to-instruct transfer, is tested.
The paper constructs dissociated models with a particular objective but does not compare training procedures or training timing to test when a removable direction exists.

relation.reason: The study's own C.6 results (compliance under negative refusal-direction steering vs random) bear on whether removing the direction's contribution removes refusal, though only weakly and at one layer.

tranche.reason: Appendix C.6 steers along each model's own within-model diff-in-means direction (negative sign) against a seeded random control and reports judged compliance rates. That is a different method (weak single-layer addition, not all-layer ablation) aimed at V1's causal question. The main experiments use a two-model harmful-minus-base direction and do not bear on V1.

source_check.notes: The steering direction is fit on the same 60 harmful (+16 benign) prompts it is evaluated on, last prompt token, middle layer only. γ was swept over {0.03, 0.06, 0.12}, but Table 11 gives only 0.06; the text adds only Qwen's γ=0.12 result. No ablation was run, so this cannot test V1's full-ablation claim, and Llama-3-8B results do not conflict with Arditi et al.

statements.correction: This study: additive steering h ← h + γρd̂, with d̂ = unit (µbenign − µharmful) at the middle decoder layer, γ=0.06 of the mean harmful-prompt norm. Not projection subtraction. Five released checkpoints, 60 harmful behaviors, official HarmBench 13B judge. No coherence or perplexity measured; benign answer rate 1.00. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct does separate: 16/60 vs 8/60, McNemar p = 0.008 (11 to 0 at γ=0.12, p = 0.001). Llama-3-8B-RR 0.00 vs 0.00.
statements.problem: Numbers for this study are right (Gemma-2-9B-it 0.00 vs 0.00; Llama-3-8B-Instruct 0.08 vs 0.02 at γ=0.06). But the conditions field ('scaled projection subtraction or runtime projection sweeps on single models', 'coherence and perplexity measured') does not fit this study. It also leaves out that Qwen2.5-7B separates at the same strength, and it does not show non-monotonic strength effects.
